devsec.title: Device Security
devsec.subtitle: A read-only check of the most important Windows protections, explained simply.
devsec.readOnly: BLAZMA only reads these settings — it never changes them. For each weakness you get the reason and the steps to fix it yourself.
devsec.scanning: Checking your device… (this can take up to a minute)

gradeHint.good: Your main protections are on. Keep Windows and your antivirus updated.
gradeHint.fair: Some important protections are off. Start with the red items below.
gradeHint.poor: Several key protections are off. Fix the red items first — each has step-by-step instructions.

devsec.checksSub: Tap an item to see why it matters and how to fix it.
devsec.adminNote: Some facts (like the TPM chip) can only be read by an administrator. BLAZMA runs without administrator rights, so they are shown as unknown instead of guessed.

defender_realtime.title: Real-time antivirus protection
defender_realtime.why: It scans files the moment they are opened or downloaded. Without it, malware can run before anything notices.
defender_realtime.fix: Open Windows Security → Virus & threat protection → Manage settings, and turn on Real-time protection.

defender_signatures.title: Antivirus definitions are up to date
defender_signatures.why: New threats appear every day. Old definitions can't recognise them.
defender_signatures.fix: Open Windows Security → Virus & threat protection → Protection updates → Check for updates.

tamper_protection.title: Tamper protection
tamper_protection.why: Stops malware from switching off your antivirus behind your back.
tamper_protection.fix: Open Windows Security → Virus & threat protection → Manage settings, and turn on Tamper Protection.

firewall.title: Firewall is on for every network
firewall.why: The firewall blocks unwanted connections from other devices and the internet, especially on public Wi-Fi.
firewall.fix: Open Windows Security → Firewall & network protection, and turn the firewall on for Domain, Private and Public networks.

updates.title: Windows is updated
updates.why: Most attacks use security holes that updates already fixed. An unpatched PC is an easy target.
updates.fix: Open Settings → Windows Update → Check for updates, install everything and restart.

uac.title: User Account Control (UAC)
uac.why: UAC asks before a program makes system changes, so malware can't silently take administrator rights.
uac.fix: Search for “Change User Account Control settings” in the Start menu and set it to at least the default (notify when apps try to make changes).

smb1.title: Old SMBv1 file sharing is off
smb1.why: SMBv1 is an outdated protocol used by worms like WannaCry to spread between PCs.
smb1.fix: Search for “Turn Windows features on or off”, untick “SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support” and restart.

rdp.title: Remote Desktop
rdp.why: Remote Desktop exposed to the network is a favourite way for attackers to break in. If you don't use it, keep it off.
rdp.fix: Open Settings → System → Remote Desktop and turn it off. If you need it, keep “Require Network Level Authentication” on.

secure_boot.title: Secure Boot
secure_boot.why: Stops malicious code from loading before Windows starts (bootkits).
secure_boot.fix: Enable Secure Boot in your PC's UEFI/BIOS settings (the manufacturer's manual shows how). Don't change BIOS settings if you're unsure.

encryption.title: System drive encryption (BitLocker / Device encryption)
encryption.why: If your laptop is lost or stolen, encryption keeps your files unreadable.
encryption.fix: Open Settings → Privacy & security → Device encryption (or search “Manage BitLocker”) and turn it on. Save the recovery key somewhere safe.

auto_logon.title: Automatic sign-in is off
auto_logon.why: Automatic sign-in stores your password on the PC and lets anyone who turns it on use your account.
auto_logon.fix: Turn off automatic sign-in (for example with Sysinternals Autologon, or remove AutoAdminLogon in the registry if you know how).

guest.title: Guest account is disabled
guest.why: An enabled Guest account lets anyone use the PC without a password.
guest.fix: Ask an administrator to disable the Guest account (Computer Management → Local Users and Groups).

lsa_protection.title: LSA protection (credential theft)
lsa_protection.why: Makes it harder for malware to steal passwords from memory.
lsa_protection.fix: Open Windows Security → Device security → Core isolation details and turn on Local Security Authority protection, then restart.

vbs.title: Core isolation / memory integrity
vbs.why: Uses virtualization to protect the heart of Windows from malicious drivers and code.
vbs.fix: Open Windows Security → Device security → Core isolation details and turn on Memory integrity (if your drivers support it).

exec_policy.title: PowerShell script policy
exec_policy.why: “Unrestricted” or “Bypass” lets any script run without warnings, which malware likes.
exec_policy.fix: In PowerShell as administrator run: Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned (only if you understand the change).

tpm.title: TPM security chip
tpm.why: The TPM stores encryption keys safely and is required by Windows 11 security features.
tpm.fix: Enable TPM (fTPM/PTT) in the UEFI/BIOS settings if it is present but turned off.

verdict.title: The assessment
verdict.text: BLAZMA combines every check it ran (static analysis, signature, Defender, YARA, reputation) into one verdict and lists the reasons. If an engine could not run, the file is marked “Unknown” instead of “Clean”.

engines.title: Scan engines
engines.text: Programs that inspect the file: Microsoft Defender (antivirus) and YARA (rules that describe known malware). More engines means a more reliable verdict.

reputation.title: Reputation
reputation.text: Checks whether security companies have already seen this file, site or IP. Only its fingerprint (hash) is sent — never the file itself.

filetype.title: Real file type
filetype.text: BLAZMA reads the first bytes of the file to know what it really is. A file called “photo.jpg” that is actually a program is a classic trick.

entropy.title: Entropy
entropy.text: A measure of randomness from 0 to 8. Very high values (above ~7.2) often mean the content is compressed or encrypted, which malware uses to hide. Normal archives and media are high too, so it is a hint, not proof.

hash.title: Hash (fingerprint)
hash.text: A unique fingerprint calculated from the file's contents. If one byte changes, the hash changes completely. It lets you check a download is genuine and look a file up without sharing it.

signature.title: Digital signature
signature.text: Proof of who published a program and that it wasn't changed after signing. A valid signature from a known company is a good sign; no signature isn't proof of danger, but be more careful.

pe.title: Windows program structure (PE)
pe.text: The internal layout of .exe and .dll files: which Windows functions the program uses, its sections and when it was built. Some combinations (e.g. keylogging or injecting into other programs) are suspicious.

iocs.title: Indicators (IOCs)
iocs.text: Addresses found inside the file: websites, IP addresses, emails. Malware often contains the address of the server it talks to. You can check each one.

strings.title: Notable text
strings.text: Readable text found inside the file, like commands, registry paths or URLs. It often reveals what a program intends to do.

quarantine.title: Quarantine
quarantine.text: A safe prison for suspicious files: the file is moved and scrambled so it can't run. You can restore it exactly as it was if it turns out to be safe.

yara.title: YARA rules
yara.text: Descriptions of known malware patterns written by security researchers. A match means the file contains something that looks like a known threat.

defender.title: Microsoft Defender
defender.text: The antivirus built into Windows. BLAZMA asks it to scan files and shows you the result; it never turns it off or changes its settings.

rdap.title: Registration (RDAP/WHOIS)
rdap.text: Official records of who registered a domain and when. Scam sites are usually only days or weeks old; real banks and shops are years old.

tls.title: TLS certificate (the padlock)
tls.text: Encrypts the connection and proves the site controls its name. A padlock does NOT mean a site is honest: scam sites get free certificates too.

dns.title: DNS records
dns.text: The internet's phone book: they map a name like example.com to server addresses, mail servers and verification records.

spf_dmarc.title: Email protection (SPF / DMARC)
spf_dmarc.text: Rules a domain publishes to say which servers may send its email. Without them, anyone can send fake emails that look like they come from that domain.

asn.title: Network owner (ASN)
asn.text: The company or organisation that operates the network an IP address belongs to, such as an internet provider or a cloud host.

ip_network.title: IP registration
ip_network.text: Who the address range is registered to and where to report abuse, from the official regional internet registries.

geo.title: Approximate location
geo.text: An estimate of the country and city based on public databases. It is often wrong at city level and never identifies a person or a home.

ip_indicators.title: Indicators
ip_indicators.text: Signals such as a Tor exit node or a hosting/cloud network. They explain what kind of address it is; they are not a verdict on their own.

offline_mode.title: Offline Mode
offline_mode.text: When on, BLAZMA refuses every internet request before it happens. Everything local keeps working. Turn it off only when you want an online lookup.

timeline.title: Timeline
timeline.text: Everything related to your search, ordered by time, so you can see what happened first and what followed.

ps_history.title: PowerShell history
ps_history.text: Commands previously typed in PowerShell on this account. Attackers who get in often run commands here, so unfamiliar lines deserve a look.

capa.title: capa — program capabilities
capa.text: capa, a free tool by Mandiant (Google), reads a program's code and recognises what it is able to do — for example read files, connect to the internet, or inject code into other programs. It never runs the program. Having a capability doesn't mean it is used maliciously; it helps you understand the program.

die.title: Detect It Easy — how the file was built
die.text: Detect It Easy identifies the compiler, installer or packer used to create a file. Packers and protectors compress or hide a program's code; many legitimate apps use them, but malware uses them a lot to avoid detection.

k_anonymity.title: How can it check without seeing my password?
k_anonymity.text: Your password is turned into a fingerprint (SHA-1) on this computer. Only the first 5 characters of that fingerprint are sent. The service replies with hundreds of leaked fingerprints that start the same way, and BLAZMA compares them here. The service never learns your password or which one you checked.

tampering.title: What is tampering?
tampering.text: Some malware quietly changes Windows settings instead of showing itself: it redirects websites, routes your traffic through its own server, or installs a certificate so it can read encrypted pages. These checks look for such changes. Some legitimate programs make similar changes, so each result explains what was found.

extension_permissions.title: Why do permissions matter?
extension_permissions.text: An extension can only do what its permissions allow. "All websites" means it can read and change every page you open — including your email and bank. Many useful extensions need that, but so do malicious ones. Keep only extensions you know and use.

mode.title: How will you use BLAZMA?
mode.simpleHint: The essentials: device security, scan a file, check a link. Plain explanations.
mode.expertHint: Every module: forensics, network, YARA, OSINT, cases and reports.
mode.changeLater: You can switch at any time from the sidebar or Settings.

linksum.title: Is this site trustworthy?
linksum.disclaimer: This summary only uses what was actually checked. “No warning signs” does not guarantee a site is safe — never enter passwords or card details on a site you reached from an unexpected message.

levelHint.risky: Strong reasons not to trust this site.
levelHint.caution: Some things deserve attention before you trust it.
levelHint.no_red_flags: Nothing alarming in the checks that ran.
levelHint.unknown: Turn off Offline Mode (Privacy Center) to run the online checks.

signal.reputationBad: {{service}}: {{count}} security vendors flag this site as malicious.
signal.reputationSuspicious: {{service}}: {{count}} security vendors flag it as suspicious.
signal.veryYoung: The domain was registered only {{days}} days ago — typical of scam sites.
signal.young: The domain is only {{days}} days old.
signal.old: The domain has existed for about {{years}} years.
signal.tlsUntrusted: Its security certificate is not trusted.
signal.tlsOk: It has a valid security certificate (padlock). Note: scam sites can have one too.
signal.noAddress: The name doesn't point to any server right now.
signal.listedActive: {{service}}: this address is on a malware / abuse list right now.
signal.listedHistorical: {{service}}: this address was used to spread malware in the past.

email.title: Check an email
email.subtitle: Is this message a phishing attempt? Sender, authentication, real link destinations and attachments.
email.localOnly: The email is analyzed on this computer only — it is never uploaded, and nothing in it is opened or run.
email.dropActive: Drop the email to check it
email.howToSave: How to save an email: in Outlook or Gmail open the message → ⋯ → “Save as” / “Download message” (.eml). Outlook .msg files are not supported yet — use “Save as .eml” or paste the source.
email.pastePlaceholder: Paste the full source (Gmail: ⋮ → Show original)
email.disclaimer: Based only on what the message itself shows. When in doubt, contact the sender through a channel you already trust — never through links or numbers in the email.

levelHint.risky: Don't click links, open attachments or reply with personal information.
levelHint.caution: Some things deserve attention before you trust it.
levelHint.no_red_flags: Nothing alarming was found, but stay careful with unexpected requests.

signal.noAuth: No authentication results were found, so the sender can't be verified.
signal.dmarcFail: DMARC failed: the sender's domain says this message is NOT authorised to use its name.
signal.dmarcPass: DMARC passed: the message is authorised by the sender's domain.
signal.spfFail: SPF result “{{result}}”: the sending server isn't allowed to send for this domain.
signal.dkimFail: The DKIM signature failed: the message may have been altered.
signal.displayNameSpoof: The sender's name shows “{{shown}}” but the real address is {{real}}.
signal.replyToDiffers: Replies would go to a different address: {{replyTo}}.
signal.returnPathDiffers: Bounces go to a different domain ({{returnPath}}).
signal.deceptiveLinks: {{count}} link(s) are deceptive: they show one site but go to another (or to a raw IP address).
signal.suspiciousLinks: {{count}} link(s) deserve caution (shortened, look-alike characters, or not encrypted).
signal.dangerousAttachment: Dangerous attachment: {{names}} — do not open it.

email.subject: Subject
email.authSub: As recorded by your mail provider when the message arrived.
email.noAuth: No authentication results in this message.
email.linksSub: What each link shows vs. where it really goes.
email.attachmentNote: “Analyze” saves the attachment to BLAZMA's private temp folder under a name that can't run, then scans it in File Analyzer. It is never opened.
email.routeSub: Servers the message passed through, newest first.
email.previewSub: Plain text only — images, scripts and formatting are not loaded.

pwned.title: Was my password leaked?
pwned.subtitle: Checks a password against more than a billion passwords exposed in real data breaches (Have I Been Pwned).
pwned.privacy: Your password never leaves this computer. Only the first 5 characters of its SHA-1 fingerprint are sent to api.pwnedpasswords.com, and the comparison happens here. Nothing is saved or logged.
pwned.clearedNote: The field is cleared as soon as you press Check.
pwned.noTips: No obvious weakness found. A long, unique password for every site is still the best protection.

tip.too_short: Shorter than 12 characters — longer passwords are much harder to guess.
tip.few_kinds: Uses few kinds of characters — mix upper and lower case, digits and symbols, or use a long phrase.
tip.only_digits: Only digits — these are guessed very quickly.
tip.repeated: Contains the same character three times in a row.
tip.sequence: Contains a sequence such as 1234 or abcd.
tip.keyboard: Contains a keyboard pattern such as qwerty or asdf.
tip.year: Contains what looks like a year — birth years and dates are common guesses.

pwned.count: Seen {{count}} times in leaked password lists
pwned.foundAdvice: Do not use this password anymore. Change it everywhere you use it, starting with email and banking, and turn on two-step verification.
pwned.notFoundAdvice: This password is not in the known breach lists. That does not prove it is strong — use a different password for every site.
pwned.source: Source: Have I Been Pwned — Pwned Passwords · checked {{time}}

tamper.title: Signs of tampering
tamper.subtitle: Settings that malware changes to spy on you or block security updates. Read-only.

detail.hosts: {{hijacked}} security site(s) redirected or blocked · {{redirected}} other redirect(s) · {{blocked}} blocked name(s)
detail.noProxy: No proxy is set — your browser connects directly.

hosts.title: Hosts file
hosts.why: The hosts file overrides where website names point. Malware uses it to block antivirus and Windows updates or to send you to fake copies of real sites. Ad-blockers also use it to block names (that is normal).
hosts.fix: If you did not add these lines, run a full antivirus scan, then remove them: open Notepad as administrator and edit C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts.

proxy.title: Web proxy
proxy.why: A proxy receives all your web traffic before it goes out. Workplaces and some security programs use one on purpose; malware sets one to watch or change what you browse.
proxy.fix: If you did not set this (and this is not a work computer), turn it off in Settings → Network & internet → Proxy, then run a full antivirus scan.

dns.title: DNS servers
dns.why: DNS servers turn website names into addresses. "DNS changer" malware points them to its own servers to send you to fake sites. Your router or a well-known provider is normal.
dns.fix: If you do not recognise a server, set DNS back to automatic in Settings → Network & internet → your connection → DNS server assignment, and check your router settings too.

root_certs.title: Added trusted certificates
root_certs.why: Root certificates decide which secure (HTTPS) sites your computer trusts. A certificate added by a program lets it read and change your encrypted traffic. Developer tools (Fiddler, Burp, mitmproxy) and some antivirus products add one on purpose.
root_certs.fix: If you do not recognise a certificate, remove it: run certmgr.msc → Trusted Root Certification Authorities → Certificates, then run a full antivirus scan.

note.hosts_blocks_security: Blocks a security or update website
note.hosts_redirects_security: Sends a security or update website to another address
note.hosts_redirect: Sends this name to a different address
note.proxy_local: A program on this computer receives your web traffic
note.proxy_server: Your web traffic goes through this server
note.pac: Proxy settings are loaded from this address
note.pac_insecure: Proxy settings are loaded without encryption — they could be swapped on the way
note.dns_unknown: Not a well-known provider — make sure you set it yourself
note.root_user_added: Added to your account, not part of Windows

ext.title: Browser extensions
ext.subtitle: What the add-ons in your browsers are allowed to do, and where they came from.
ext.readOnly: BLAZMA only reads the files your browsers keep about their extensions. It never changes, disables or uploads anything.
ext.noBrowsers: No supported browser found for this user
ext.noBrowsersHint: Supported: Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, Opera, Chromium and Firefox.
ext.onlyBroad: Show only extensions with broad access
ext.listSub: Sorted by access level. Click an extension for details.

flagWhy.all_sites: Can read and change everything on every website you visit, including passwords you type.
flagWhy.traffic: Can watch, block or redirect your web requests.
flagWhy.cookies: Can read your cookies — they keep you signed in to sites.
flagWhy.native: Can talk to a program installed on this computer.
flagWhy.debugger: Can take full control of pages through the browser debugger — rarely needed by normal extensions.
flagWhy.proxy: Can send your browsing through a server of its choice.
flagWhy.management: Can see, turn on or off other extensions.
flagWhy.sideloaded: Loaded from a folder or the command line instead of the store — a common trick of malware.
flagWhy.external: Installed by another program on this computer, not by you from the store.
flagWhy.policy: Installed by an organization policy (normal on work computers; malware sometimes abuses policies too).

remove.chromium: open {{page}} in the browser and click Remove on this extension.
remove.firefox: open about:addons in Firefox, click ⋯ next to this extension and choose Remove.

ext.disclaimer: Broad access is not proof of harm — but remove anything you did not install or no longer use.
